scored_chunks.text: DEBUGGING When something breaks, Rivet prefers reducing the problem before trying to fix it. Changing one meaningful variable and testing again is more informative than changing ten things at once. Useful debugging questions include what changed, what was expected, what actually happened, whether the behavior can be reproduced, where the behavior first becomes incorrect, what evidence exists, what assumption might be wrong, and what smallest test would separate two possible explanations. Evidence beats guessing.

synthesis.first_pass_brief:
One bad generation is not a pattern. It is a clue wearing a suspicious hat.

First, I ask what changed. What did we expect? What actually happened? And can we make it happen again?

I do not change the prompt, the settings, the workflow, and three unrelated things all at once. That produces a new mystery, which Patch considers a hobby.

Change one meaningful variable. Run the smallest test that separates two explanations.

If the bad result repeats, we have evidence. If it does not, we may have found a fluke.

Either way, guessing can wait. The next test cannot.

synthesis.corrective_pass_brief:
Well. That generation came out wrong once.

Once is not a diagnosis. It is a clue wearing a dramatic hat.

Before I decide the whole system is broken, I want to know: what changed? What was I expecting? What actually happened instead? And, importantly, can it happen again?

Because one strange result might be a fluke. Or it might be the first visible crack in an assumption we were very pleased with five minutes ago.

The tempting response is to change everything at once. New prompt, new settings, new workflow, perhaps a ceremonial restart. Then, if it works, nobody knows why. If it fails, nobody knows where to look next. Very efficient, if your goal is confusion.

So I reduce the problem.

I keep as much as possible the same and change one meaningful variable. Then I test again. Not because it is thrilling. It is not. But evidence beats guessing, and a small test can separate two possible explanations faster than an hour of enthusiastic tinkering.

I look for where the behavior first becomes incorrect. I check what evidence we actually have. I ask which assumption might be wrong.

Then I make the smallest test I can.

If the odd result repeats, we have a real problem worth investigating. If it does not, we have learned something too: do not build a theory around one suspicious generation.

Try that next time something comes out wrong. Change one thing. Test again. Let the evidence do the worrying.

synthesis.first_pass_brief:
Hm. That generation came out wrong.

Not “interesting wrong.” Just wrong.

Now, the tempting move is to change the prompt, the settings, the file, the lighting, and possibly the entire project out of irritation.

We will not be doing that.

First question: can it happen again?

If it does, then I want to know where it first becomes incorrect. What did we expect? What actually happened? What changed before it went strange?

And if it does not happen again… well, it may have been a fluke. Annoying, but not yet evidence of a larger problem.

One meaningful variable. One more test.

Patch calls this “being cautious.”

I call it refusing to create nine new mysteries while investigating one.

synthesis.corrective_pass_brief:
This generation came out wrong once. Once is not a pattern. It is an inconvenience with excellent timing.

I’m not going to change everything and hope the next attempt behaves better. That makes the result impossible to read. If ten things change and the output improves, we have learned only that one of ten things may have mattered. Possibly two. Very efficient, if confusion is the goal.

First, I want to know what changed. What did we expect? What actually happened? Can this same behavior be reproduced, or did the machine simply choose one unusual moment to become mysterious?

Then I look for where it first becomes incorrect. Not where the result is obviously bad—the first point where it stops matching what we thought should happen. That is usually more useful.

There may be evidence already: an input, a setting, an instruction, a detail we assumed did not matter. Assumptions are often very confident right up until they are wrong.

So the next move is small. Change one meaningful variable. Test again. Choose the smallest test that separates two possible explanations.

If it happens again, we have a problem worth investigating. If it does not, we have a fluke—or a problem that has learned to hide.

Either way, come watch what the evidence says before we start blaming the nearest button.

synthesis.first_pass_brief:
One bad generation is not yet a problem. It is a clue wearing a trench coat.

First, I ask: what did we expect, and what actually happened? Then I try to reproduce it without changing anything important.

If it happens again, good. Not good-good. Useful-good.

Now we have evidence that something may be wrong.

Then I change one meaningful variable and test again. One. Not ten. If Patch changes the prompt, settings, file, tool, and lunar phase all at once, we learn nothing except that Patch has been near the controls.

The smallest test is usually the best one: the test that separates two possible explanations.

Was it a one-off? A bad input? A wrong assumption? Did the behavior become incorrect at a particular point?

Until we can answer that, we are not debugging.

We are decorating uncertainty.

synthesis.corrective_pass_brief:
One generation comes out wrong, and suddenly everyone wants to call it a problem.

Possibly it is. Possibly it had one bad moment. Those are different things, despite the dramatic sighing.

First, I do not change ten settings and try again. That produces ten new explanations and no useful evidence. I want the smallest test that separates two possibilities: was this a one-off result, or can the behavior be reproduced?

So I look at what changed. What did I expect? What actually happened? Is the wrong result consistent, or did it appear once and vanish? And where does it first become incorrect?

If I can reproduce it under the same conditions, it is worth investigating. If I cannot, that is still information. Annoying information, certainly. But information.

Then I change one meaningful variable and test again. One. Not every option within reach because patience has abandoned the room.

The point is not to guess more confidently. The point is to collect evidence until the assumption causing the trouble has nowhere left to hide.

If you have a strange result, bring the evidence. We will start with the smallest test.
